title: Validation Master Plan, URS and Risk Assessment

lessons.title: Plan before you qualify
lessons.objective: Connect a manufacturing need to evidence and an authorized decision.

scenes.title: Start with the intended use
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module Two. Our fictional project is a jacketed mixing vessel used to prepare an aqueous oral solution before filling. It is not an aseptic process. We will follow the project from planning to a review decision. Begin by asking what product the system supports, how it will be used, and what could go wrong. A polished protocol cannot rescue an undefined purpose.

scenes.title: Three connected documents
scenes.narration: The validation master plan describes the programme. The user requirements specification describes what the system must do. The risk assessment explains where failures matter and how controls will be justified. In this course we say V M P and U R S. These documents should agree with one another. If the vessel needs controlled mixing, the requirement, risk discussion and verification evidence should all address that need.

scenes.title: The evidence journey
scenes.narration: Imagine buying a vessel because the catalogue says pharmaceutical grade. That description does not establish fitness for our product. The team still needs to understand contact materials, cleaning, measurement, mixing and records. The illustration connects a product vessel to its temperature sensor and control panel. These are functional interfaces, not a construction drawing. The same intended use must guide design review, testing and routine operation.

scenes.title: Your first decision
scenes.narration: For the first activity, describe the vessel's intended use in three sentences. Identify the product family, operating purpose and important interfaces. Then list information that is still missing. Do not invent operating limits to complete a form. Assign each missing item to an appropriate owner, such as process development or engineering. Planning is useful when it exposes uncertainty early enough to change the project.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest starting point?
options: A defined intended use with product context
quiz.feedback: Intended use provides the basis for requirements and evidence; a brochure or signature alone does not.

lessons.activity: Write a three-sentence intended-use statement and identify three unknowns.
lessons.model: Example: vessel V-201 prepares a defined aqueous oral-solution product family before transfer to filling. It mixes within the established batch-volume range and interfaces with approved utilities and a controlled transfer path. Confirm viscosity range, cleaning strategy and required measurement performance with their owners.

lessons.title: Build a useful validation master plan
lessons.objective: Distinguish programme governance from a protocol and a schedule.

scenes.title: A map, not a pile of protocols
scenes.narration: A useful validation master plan helps a new team member understand how qualification and validation are governed. In European Union GMP Annex Fifteen, the programme may be defined in a V M P or equivalent document. This is not a requirement to give every site the same template. Our worked plan is a teaching structure. The applicable quality system determines the authorized document structure and approval responsibilities.

scenes.title: Make scope visible
scenes.narration: For our small oral-liquid project, the plan links the mixing vessel, transfer equipment, utilities and supporting procedures. A scope table records the system identifier, intended use, responsible owner and current evidence status. An entry called complete without a report reference is difficult to challenge. An explicit status such as design review pending tells the team what still needs to happen. A date in a schedule is not proof of qualification.

scenes.title: Separate the documents
scenes.narration: The programme plan explains the approach and oversight. A protocol states how a particular verification will be performed and judged. A report evaluates what actually happened. The diagram presents these as connected documents rather than interchangeable files. For example, the plan may require risk-informed testing; the protocol specifies a particular mixing test; the report evaluates the observed results and any deviations.

scenes.title: Review the living programme
scenes.narration: Now suppose the project adds a second product with different cleaning needs. Reusing the original plan unchanged may conceal a new scope. Compare the new use with the approved assumptions, identify the affected systems, and route updates through the quality system. In the activity, prepare a short programme outline with owners, document references and review triggers. A useful plan should help people act, not merely describe intentions.

quiz.question: Which record demonstrates what happened during a test?
options: The executed record and evaluated report
quiz.feedback: The plan and quotation describe intentions; executed records and the report provide evidence and evaluation.

lessons.activity: Draft a one-page programme outline with scope, ownership, document hierarchy and three review triggers.
lessons.model: Include the project purpose, V-201 and its interfaces, engineering and quality responsibilities, links to requirements and protocols, deviation/change routes, status reporting and review after product change, significant modification or adverse performance.

lessons.title: System boundaries and responsibilities
lessons.objective: Identify interfaces and avoid gaps between teams.

scenes.title: Draw the boundary
scenes.narration: A system boundary is a practical agreement about what is included in the assessment. Our vessel receives product materials and a heating or cooling service, and transfers bulk solution downstream. The simplified diagram shows these interfaces. It does not assert that the utility is qualified by qualifying the vessel. Each interface needs an owner and a clear connection to the evidence for the supplying or receiving system.

scenes.title: Consider indirect effects
scenes.narration: A component does not need to touch product to affect quality. A temperature sensor sends information to a controller, which can influence the jacket service and therefore the product. Conversely, physical proximity alone does not make every room object equally important. Describe the mechanism by which a component failure could affect the process. Use that explanation to support scope decisions rather than relying only on a label such as critical.

scenes.title: Assign decisions explicitly
scenes.narration: Engineering understands the design and installation. Operations understands how people use and clean the equipment. Quality oversight connects decisions to the pharmaceutical quality system. Additional expertise may be needed from development, microbiology, metrology or information technology. This is a suggested team for the fictional project, not a universal organizational chart. Identify who prepares evidence, who reviews it and who has authority to approve each decision.

scenes.title: Find the missing interface
scenes.narration: Review this handover: the vessel report is ready, but the transfer hose has no approved cleaning procedure and the utility connection is not identified. Calling the vessel ready for routine use would hide unresolved interfaces. Record the gaps and assess their impact. For the activity, draw a boundary and assign an owner to each interface. A boundary is useful only when work outside it has somewhere explicit to go.

quiz.question: Can a non-product-contact sensor affect product quality?
options: Yes, through the process it controls
quiz.feedback: An indirect control pathway can affect quality even without product contact.

lessons.activity: Draw four interfaces for V-201 and assign an owner and evidence reference to each.
lessons.model: Consider jacket utility supply, temperature measurement, incoming materials and transfer hose. Reference the relevant utility status, calibration evidence, material controls and cleaning verification. Flag missing evidence rather than assigning an assumed pass.

lessons.title: Write testable user requirements
lessons.objective: Turn vague purchase language into verifiable requirements.

scenes.title: From adjective to requirement
scenes.narration: A user requirement should communicate an actual need. The phrase easy to clean is useful as a concern but too vague to verify on its own. Ask what product residues are expected, which surfaces must be accessible, what cleaning process is intended and how the design will support it. Do not insert a universal surface finish or residue limit simply because another project used it. The scientific basis belongs to the actual application.

scenes.title: One requirement, one trace
scenes.narration: For our fictional example, requirement U R S zero one states that product-contact materials must be identified and supported by approved compatibility evidence for the defined product and cleaning agents. The design review checks the proposed materials. Later verification checks the installed materials and supporting records. The requirement has an identifier, a clear subject and an evidence path. The site defines the actual acceptance criteria and document controls.

scenes.title: An illustrative measurable need
scenes.narration: Consider a training-only temperature indication requirement: within the selected operating range, indication error must remain within a project-defined tolerance when compared with a suitable calibrated reference. The range and tolerance are not supplied here because the process basis is still missing. This is a deliberate unresolved requirement, not a pass. The exercise asks you to identify the information needed to finalize it before procurement or testing.

scenes.title: Control revisions
scenes.narration: Requirements evolve as knowledge improves, but uncontrolled changes break traceability. If the intended batch range changes, assess effects on mixing, measurement, cleaning and verification. Retain the reason for the revision and the approval trail. Do not silently edit a requirement after a failed test to make the result pass. In the activity, rewrite three vague statements and clearly mark any assumptions that require resolution.

quiz.question: A test fails the approved requirement. What is appropriate?
options: Document and assess the failure through controlled procedures
quiz.feedback: A failed result needs documented evaluation; a requirement change must be justified and controlled.

lessons.activity: Rewrite “accurate sensor”, “easy to clean” and “secure records” into verifiable requirements with unresolved inputs marked.
lessons.model: Define the measured variable, intended range, justified tolerance and comparison method; define cleaning access and compatibility evidence; define authorized access, attributable records and retention/retrieval needs. Do not invent site limits.

lessons.title: Trace requirements into verification
lessons.objective: Follow a requirement from design to objective evidence.

scenes.title: Build a traceability chain
scenes.narration: A traceability matrix is a practical teaching tool for connecting needs to evidence. Each row links a requirement to its design response, relevant risk control, verification activity and result. A check mark is not enough if the underlying record cannot be located. For our vessel, the product-contact-material requirement links to a design specification, installed material records and the review that confirms suitability for the intended use.

scenes.title: Distinguish planned and verified
scenes.narration: The three cards show different states. A planned test has an approved method but no result. An executed test has observations, which may include a failure. An accepted result has been evaluated against the applicable criteria with deviations addressed appropriately. Keeping these states separate prevents a dashboard from showing green simply because someone uploaded a file. The evidence must answer the requirement, not merely share its title.

scenes.title: Supplier evidence needs context
scenes.narration: A supplier may provide useful testing and design records. Review whether they apply to the purchased configuration, use appropriate methods and preserve reliable data. Transport, installation or configuration changes can affect whether a result remains applicable. Our example is a factory test of an alarm that depends on a site-installed sensor. The team must assess what needs verification after installation. A supplier signature does not settle that question automatically.

scenes.title: Close the gaps
scenes.narration: In the activity, construct five traceability rows. Mark the status honestly and identify the next action for each gap. A requirement with no test may need a new verification method. A test with no requirement may reveal an undocumented need or unnecessary work. Traceability should support technical thinking in both directions. It is a means of exposing missing evidence, not a substitute for judging whether that evidence is adequate.

quiz.question: Does an executed test necessarily mean an accepted requirement?
options: No, results and deviations still need evaluation
Only if the file is signed by the vendor
quiz.feedback: Execution and acceptance are distinct; evidence must meet criteria and receive the appropriate evaluation.

lessons.activity: Create five requirement-to-evidence rows using the downloadable traceability worksheet.
lessons.model: Include materials, measurement, mixing range, cleaning and records. Give each an ID, design response, verification method, evidence reference, status and open action. Use pending where evidence is absent.

lessons.title: Ask a precise risk question
lessons.objective: Separate hazard, failure mode, harm and uncertainty.

scenes.title: Define the question
scenes.narration: For this project, ask: could inadequate mixing within the intended batch range lead to non-uniform product before transfer? This is more useful than asking whether the vessel is risky. The question identifies a possible failure, product consequence and operating context. Our diagram shows the possible chain from lost mixing to variable concentration and a potentially affected dose. It is not measured process data and does not prove that any real vessel performs poorly.

scenes.title: Separate the concepts
scenes.narration: A stopped agitator is a failure mode. Non-uniform concentration may be a product-quality effect, depending on the formulation and process. An incorrect delivered dose may be a patient consequence. These links require scientific understanding; they are not automatic for every liquid. The exercise asks you to explain the chain and list the evidence needed to judge it. Avoid assigning a score before you understand the scenario.

scenes.title: Make uncertainty visible
scenes.narration: ICH Q Nine revision one links risk decisions to scientific knowledge and patient protection. The degree of formality should reflect risk, uncertainty, importance and complexity. For our case, a small development study may not represent the full batch range. Record that limitation and plan how to reduce uncertainty. A low number based on a guess is not stronger evidence than a clearly stated unknown.

scenes.title: Choose the right discussion
scenes.narration: Invite people who understand the process, equipment and potential consequences. Ask each person which assumptions could be wrong and what evidence would change the decision. If the project deadline is influencing scores, make that bias explicit. In the activity, write one risk question and one cause-to-harm chain. Keep the language specific enough that another reviewer can disagree with it constructively and identify what needs checking.

quiz.question: What should come before assigning a risk score?
options: Defining the failure scenario and evidence
quiz.feedback: A meaningful score depends on a well-defined scenario and an evidence-based rationale.

lessons.activity: Write a risk question for mixing and another for cleaning; identify one uncertainty in each.
lessons.model: Example: could incomplete drainage after cleaning retain residue that affects the next product? Clarify residue characteristics, equipment geometry and cleaning evidence. Mixing uncertainty may involve viscosity or batch-volume range.

lessons.title: Use FMEA without false precision
lessons.objective: Apply a transparent scoring exercise and recognize its limits.

scenes.title: A tool, not the decision
scenes.narration: Failure mode and effects analysis, often called F M E A, can organize a discussion. This course uses a fictional three-level scale for severity, occurrence and difficulty of detection. These numbers are ordinal teaching categories, not measured probabilities. They are not official regulatory limits. The interactive exercise makes the arithmetic visible while keeping the rationale and unresolved high-severity concerns beside the result.

scenes.title: Define the scales first
scenes.narration: In this exercise, higher severity means more serious potential harm. Higher occurrence means the failure is more plausible given the available evidence. Higher detection score means it is harder to discover the failure before its consequence. Real projects need operational definitions tailored to the scenario. A team should agree those definitions before scoring. The labels lower and higher alone are not sufficient for an approved site assessment.

scenes.title: Equal products, different stories
scenes.narration: Multiply three by one by two and the result is six. Multiply one by three by two and the result is also six. Yet the first scenario has a higher severity category. The chart shows equal total scores with different component patterns. Equal products do not establish equivalent risk or acceptable controls. Review the scenario, severity, uncertainty and control options rather than letting one number decide.

scenes.title: Re-score after evidence
scenes.narration: Suppose an independent alarm is proposed. Do not lower the detection score merely because the alarm appears on a drawing. Determine whether it detects the relevant failure, whether someone will respond and whether that response is timely. Verify the control and reassess residual risk. The activity asks you to compare two scoring rationales and explain which assumptions need evidence. No score in this lesson automatically authorizes release.

quiz.question: Two scenarios have the same multiplied score. Are their risks equivalent?
options: Yes, if the spreadsheet is protected
Not necessarily; component scores and context matter
quiz.feedback: Equal products can conceal different severity, uncertainty and control needs.

lessons.activity: Use the interactive score explorer. Compare 3×1×2 with 1×3×2 and explain why a single threshold is insufficient.
lessons.model: Both equal 6, but severity differs. Prioritize the full failure scenario and evidence; examine uncertainty and control effectiveness. Do not infer an official acceptance threshold from the exercise.

lessons.title: Turn risk controls into testable actions
lessons.objective: Connect proposed controls to owners and evidence.

scenes.title: Prefer a clear mechanism
scenes.narration: A control should explain how it changes the failure pathway. Prevention reduces the chance of failure. Detection identifies a problem. Response determines what happens next. For a mixing failure, a justified design or operating control may prevent an unsuitable condition. An alarm may detect it, but only an effective response can limit the consequence. The three blocks are complementary; none is automatically adequate for every process.

scenes.title: Assign an owner and proof
scenes.narration: Our fictional action is to verify the agitator-status indication and the defined response to loss of mixing. Engineering owns the technical check and operations owns the response procedure and training. The verification plan records the challenge method and the expected behaviour. Quality oversight reviews the evidence through the site system. Action closed should mean the intended result was demonstrated, not merely that a document was drafted.

scenes.title: Look for new failure paths
scenes.narration: Adding a control can introduce a new dependency. An alarm may depend on power, configuration, sensor health or a shared signal. If the alarm and controller use the same failed sensor, apparent independence may be misleading. The diagram shows a common sensor feeding two functions to make that concern visible. Examine the actual architecture and challenge assumptions before taking credit for an independent protective layer.

scenes.title: Residual risk is a decision
scenes.narration: After controls are implemented, evaluate what risk remains and who can accept it. Record assumptions and review triggers. Quality risk management does not excuse a practice that conflicts with applicable requirements. For the activity, select one failure mode and propose a prevention, detection and response strategy. Then identify evidence for effectiveness and one new risk introduced by your proposal. This turns a list of actions into an auditable argument.

quiz.question: When can a proposed alarm receive credit as an effective control?
options: As soon as it is purchased
After appropriate effectiveness evidence and evaluation
quiz.feedback: The control must address the failure and work in context; purchase or proposal alone is insufficient.

lessons.activity: Write one control plan with an owner, verification method, completion evidence and review trigger.
lessons.model: For loss of mixing, consider suitable design/operating controls, status detection and a defined product-impact response. Verify the signal, alarm and response assumptions; assess common-cause failures and document residual risk.

lessons.title: Read data before declaring success
lessons.objective: Interpret a small illustrative dataset without overclaiming.

scenes.title: A deliberately small dataset
scenes.narration: The learning dashboard contains ten fictional temperature-indication errors in degrees Celsius: zero point one, zero point two, zero point one, zero point three, zero point two, zero point four, zero point three, zero point five, zero point four and zero point six. They illustrate a time-ordered pattern. They are not calibration data from a real instrument and do not define a pharmaceutical tolerance.

scenes.title: Calculate transparently
scenes.narration: The total is three point one degrees across ten errors, giving a mean error of zero point three one degrees. The range is zero point six minus zero point one, or zero point five degrees. The highest error is zero point six degrees. The chart includes the underlying values in a table so that learners can check the arithmetic without relying on colour or vision. These summaries describe this small dataset only.

scenes.title: Pass limits are not trend limits
scenes.narration: For arithmetic practice only, set an illustrative absolute-error limit of zero point five degrees. Nine of the ten observations meet that example limit and one does not. The limit is not an official criterion and does not qualify an instrument. The upward pattern also deserves attention even before a limit is exceeded. In a real investigation, examine measurement uncertainty, reference suitability, conditions and data integrity before drawing conclusions.

scenes.title: Do not infer capability
scenes.narration: Do not calculate a confident capability claim from these ten convenient values. A meaningful analysis requires a suitable study design and understanding of the measurement system and process behaviour. In the activity, change the illustrative limit, observe the count and explain what information is still missing. More green points do not create more knowledge. The purpose is to practice transparent calculation and proportionate interpretation, not to approve a system.

quiz.question: What can these ten fictional values establish?
options: A descriptive summary for the exercise
quiz.feedback: They support the stated arithmetic exercise, not qualification, capability or regulatory acceptance.

lessons.activity: Calculate the mean and range, count results above 0.5 °C, and list four missing inputs before a real decision.
lessons.model: Mean 0.31 °C; range 0.50 °C; one value exceeds 0.5 °C. Missing inputs include justified acceptance criteria, reference/measurement uncertainty, operating conditions and representative study design.

lessons.title: Capstone: make a defensible handover decision
lessons.objective: Integrate the plan, requirements, risks and evidence.

scenes.title: The review packet
scenes.narration: You are reviewing the fictional V two zero one handover. The intended use is documented and the material records are available. However, the required mixing range has not been finalized, the transfer-hose cleaning evidence is missing and the alarm response has not been verified. A dashboard says ninety percent complete. Your task is to decide what the evidence supports, not to maximize the completion percentage.

scenes.title: Separate project progress from readiness
scenes.narration: A percentage can be useful for scheduling, but it treats unlike activities as if they were interchangeable. Finishing several minor tasks does not offset an unresolved requirement that affects product quality. The visual compares a large completion bar with three named gaps. Read the gaps directly: mixing range, cleaning evidence and alarm response. Their significance must be evaluated individually in the context of the intended use.

scenes.title: Write a reasoned decision
scenes.narration: For this exercise, routine-use readiness is not demonstrated. State that conclusion, identify the missing evidence, assign owners and define what must be reviewed before a new decision. If a project proposes progression to a limited next stage, assess that specific activity and its dependencies separately through the approved system. Do not describe conditional progression as general permission for production. The scope of an authorization must be unambiguous.

scenes.title: Carry the method forward
scenes.narration: Complete the workbook and final assessment, then compare your capstone with the model reasoning. You should now be able to explain the purpose of the programme plan, draft testable requirements, connect them to evidence and discuss risk without hiding behind scores. These self-study results are not a formal qualification or competency record. Apply the method with qualified colleagues, current requirements and approved site procedures when working on a real project.

quiz.question: The packet is 90% complete but critical evidence is missing. What follows?
options: Approve because most tasks are done
Readiness is not demonstrated; evaluate and resolve the gaps
quiz.feedback: Completion percentage cannot replace evaluation of important unresolved evidence.

lessons.activity: Prepare a one-page handover decision with evidence, gaps, owners, actions and conditions for reconsideration.
lessons.model: Routine-use readiness is not demonstrated. Resolve the mixing-range basis, transfer-cleaning evidence and alarm-response verification with named functions and controlled records. Reassess risk/traceability and seek the applicable authorized decision. Do not invent signatures.
